sentences.text: Yandusaurus hongheensis is the sole known species of this extinct ornithopod, a group of herbivorous dinosaurs that lived approximately 165 million years ago in Asia.
Its fifteen maxillary teeth were largest in the middle and overlapped, featuring a unique pattern of parallel vertical ridges that researchers compared to the fingers of Buddha statues.

Juvenile specimens were small bipedal runners measuring between 1 and 1.6 meters in length, 70 centimeters in height, and weighing around 7 kilograms, while the adult possessed large eyes indicated by the curved jugal bone.
The holotype skeleton was accidentally processed by a composter during construction work in January 1973 near the Honghe dam in Sichuan, China.
The genus name Yandusaurus is derived from Yandu, the ancient name for Zigong, which means 'salt capital' due to the area's history of salt mining.

The holotype specimen GCC V20501 was excavated from the Lower Shaximiao Formation and consists of a partial skeleton with a skull, vertebral column, shoulder girdle, and limbs, though most elements are limited or damaged.
Professor He Xinlu named and described the type species Yandusaurus hongheensis in 1979, after it was initially misidentified locally as Yubasaurus or Honghesaurus.
Yandusaurus is currently viewed as having an unresolved position within Neornithischia, as its original family Hypsilophodontidae is considered paraphyletic.
In 1992, Guangzhao Peng reassigned Yandusaurus multidens to the genus Agilisaurus, and in 2005, Paul Barrett and colleagues placed Yandusaurus multidens in its own genus, Hexinlusaurus.

Yandusaurus lived during the Middle Jurassic, specifically the Bathonian age between 168 and 162 million years ago, in eastern Asia, with fossil occurrences also recorded from the Bajocian stage between 170.9 and 168.2 million years ago.
